Foreign investors pulled their money out of Indian markets, even though domestic institutions stepped in with some defensive buying.
Upcoming events like the US Federal Reserve meeting, industrial production metrics, and second-quarter corporate earnings will drive the market's next moves.
analysis.what_happened: Indian stocks faced selling pressure because crude oil prices jumped due to Middle East tensions, and foreign investors pulled money out. Markets are now looking ahead to the US Federal Reserve meeting and company earnings reports to see where things go next.
analysis.analogy: It is like a sports team losing its rhythm because the weather turned stormy and the star players (foreign investors) decided to sit out, leaving the home team to struggle against rising pressure.
why_it_matters_india: Middle East tensions push up crude oil prices -> India has to spend more dollars to buy oil
Higher oil import costs and foreign investors pulling money out -> puts downward pressure on the rupee
Foreign investors selling Indian stocks -> causes stock market indices like the Nifty to drop
Upcoming US Federal Reserve decisions and local corporate earnings -> will dictate whether market sentiment recovers or stays fearful

impacts.rationale: Selling pressure from foreign investors and rising oil risks push the main market index down, which means lower portfolio values for investors in the short term.

When foreign investors pull money out and crude oil costs rise, the rupee weakens (each rupee buys fewer dollars), making imported goods like electronics and fuel more expensive for everyday consumers.
Soaring crude oil prices due to Middle East tensions typically translate to higher fuel costs at the pump, increasing transport and daily living expenses.

events.headline: Record Tanker Rates Cripple U.S. Crude Oil Flows to Asia

items.title: Record Tanker Rates Cripple U.S. Crude Oil Flows to Asia
items.summary: The Iran war has made oil tanker voyages so inefficient that vessel availability has crumbled and freight costs have soared to record-highs, all but erasing the incentive for shipping crude oil from the U.S. Gulf Coast to Asia. The cost of shipping crude oil from the U.S. Gulf Coast to China soared to as high as $80 million earlier this month. That’s ten times the average tanker rates that had held for years before the Iran war. Freight rates have eased from the record highs seen in early October, but they were still about $60 million for…

events.article_text:
U.S. Dips Into Strategic Oil Reserve Again Amid Supply Disruptions

What I Cover Tsvetana Paraskova is an energy and commodities journalist who has contributed to Oilprice.com for nearly a decade, covering global energy markets, commodities,…

The Iran war has made oil tanker voyages so inefficient that vessel availability has crumbled and freight costs have soared to record-highs, all but erasing the incentive for shipping crude oil from the U.S. Gulf Coast to Asia.

The cost of shipping crude oil from the U.S. Gulf Coast to China soared to as high as $80 million earlier this month. That’s ten times the average tanker rates that had held for years before the Iran war.

Freight rates have eased from the record highs seen in early October, but they were still about $60 million for a supertanker to carry oil from the U.S. to Asia this week. The cost is so high that Asian refiners aren’t ordering much crude from the U.S. for November delivery.

So far this month, Asian refiner orders for U.S. crude have plunged by about 50% from September, to about 25 million barrels that would be delivered in November, anonymous traders familiar with the purchasing told Bloomberg.

If orders remain so low for the rest of this monthly trading cycle, Asia could receive in November its lowest volumes of U.S. crude oil in seven years, according to vessel-tracking analysts. Related: The Hidden $40-Per-Barrel Cost Driving Oil Prices Higher

U.S. crude oil and petroleum exports surged to a record high in the early weeks of the Middle East war. But the conflict and attempts by Middle Eastern producers to move oil out of the Strait of Hormuz broke the global tanker market and added a shipping crisis on top of the oil supply and fuel crises.

The Iran war has reshuffled trade routes and patterns and tied up more tankers in inefficient and lengthy voyages.

The increased flows of oil from the Strait of Hormuz, mostly thanks to ship-to-ship (STS) transfers in the Gulf of Oman, are tying up supertankers for weeks waiting for the transfers outside the Strait, limiting the availability of very large crude carriers (VLCCs) for the other global key oil trade routes, such as the U.S. Gulf Coast to Asia.

The Gulf of Oman shuttle fleet has expanded to about 80 VLCCs. However, the average round-voyage times have reached 23 days, more than double the optimal 9–10 days for a round trip from Basrah in Iraq to Sohar offshore Oman, according to Kpler.

Moreover, record rates to ship crude out of the Persian Gulf and from the Gulf of Oman are luring tankers to the risky but very lucrative Middle East trade, leaving the market short on vessels elsewhere.

Freight rates are now the main story on the market, Randy Hawkins, Vice President, International Crude Oil Supply and Trading at Valero Energy, said on the U.S. refiner’s earnings call this week.

“The cost to move a VLCC from the Gulf Coast to Asia is now averaging around 30 to $35 per barrel. That compares with the 2025 average of around $5 a barrel,” Hawkins said.

The freight cost surge is “causing severe dislocations in our global crude pricing as refiners seek to find barrels that are closer to home and sellers are forced to discount barrels to account for the freight cost.”

Asian buyers are turning to more Middle East crude, but they are buying on a delivered basis to reduce costs.

In Europe, refiners are opting for nearby volumes within the region, due to the spike in tanker rates.

The higher demand for European and Middle Eastern crude is pushing up the premiums on some grades. The Dated Brent benchmark was at a record $20 per barrel premium to Brent last week. Norway’s medium sour crude Johan Sverdrup has hit a record $24 per barrel premium to Brent, according to Wood Mackenzie data.

African and U.S. crudes, on the other hand, have seen premiums tumbling and discounts widening due to the high freight costs to ship these volumes on long voyages to Asia. West African crude prices have slumped to record-low discounts, with some grades down to minus $20 per barrel to offset the high shipping costs.

In the U.S. market, the premium of WTI at the Midland East Houston (MEH) hub has slumped to $0.25 a barrel above WTI, from over $3 per barrel premium in early September, per estimates by Link Data Services cited by Bloomberg.

The U.S. Gulf of Mexico’s medium-sour Mars crude, similar to many Middle Eastern grades, saw its premium tumble to $6 a barrel, down from $17.50 at the end of March.

analysis.tldr: Soaring shipping costs from the Iran war are making oil transport too expensive, pushing up global energy prices and risking costlier fuel and imports for India.
the_story: The Iran war has caused oil tanker voyages to become inefficient, pushing shipping costs for a supertanker from the U.S. Gulf Coast to Asia up to record highs of $80 million earlier this month and settling around $60 million this week.
Asian refiners' orders for U.S. crude oil plunged by about 50% in October compared to September, down to roughly 25 million barrels for November delivery.
Ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman are tying up about 80 supertankers, stretching round-voyage times to 23 days and draining ship availability for other global routes like the U.S. to Asia.

Refiners in Asia and Europe are shifting to nearby oil supplies, causing prices for regional grades like Dated Brent and Norway's Johan Sverdrup to hit record premiums while U.S. and African crude prices are heavily discounted.
analysis.what_happened: A war involving Iran has disrupted global shipping routes, tying up giant oil tankers (VLCCs) near the Middle East for weeks-long transfers instead of normal travel. Because ships are scarce and stuck, the cost to charter a vessel to carry oil has multiplied tenfold, making it unprofitable for Asian buyers to purchase crude oil shipped from the U.S.
analysis.analogy: It is like delivery vans suddenly charging ten times the usual price because they are stuck in massive traffic jams around one hub, forcing local shops to abandon faraway suppliers and buy expensive produce from closer neighbors instead.
why_it_matters_india: The Iran war and congested Middle East shipping routes force tankers into long, inefficient voyages.
A shortage of available ships causes global shipping and freight costs to soar to record highs.
Soaring transport expenses disrupt global oil trade flows, pushing refiners to scramble for nearby energy supplies and driving up specific oil benchmark premiums.

Higher global crude and shipping costs ripple through to India—a major oil importer—potentially raising local fuel costs, driving up inflation, and putting pressure on the rupee (each rupee buys fewer dollars).

impacts.rationale: higher global oil and transport costs make importing and refining energy more expensive for India, pushing up everyday goods and transport prices—bad for consumers.
costlier imported oil means India has to spend more dollars to buy energy, weakening the local currency—bad for importers and travelers.
ongoing Middle East conflict and global shipping chaos drive investors toward safe-haven assets, pushing up global and domestic gold prices — good for current holders, bad for buyers.
spiking international crude and shipping expenses eventually translate into costlier pump prices for everyday motorists in India.

watch_next: Whether tanker freight rates in the Middle East begin to ease or stay at record highs
Changes in Asian refiner demand and whether they continue to shun long-distance U.S. oil shipments
analysis.caveats: If tanker availability recovers faster than expected, shipping costs could drop and normalize global oil trade routes.

items.title: India's basmati rice yield likely to be 5-10% higher this year: Industry leader
items.summary: Rajeev Setia, President of Basmati IREF and Joint MD of Chaman Lal Setia Exports, said the monsoon and rainfall supported basmati growth and higher yields

items.title: India's basmati rice yield likely to be 5-10% higher this year: Industry leader
items.summary: Rajeev Setia, President of Basmati IREF and Joint MD of Chaman Lal Setia Exports, said the monsoon and rainfall supported basmati growth and higher yields

events.article_text:
India's basmati rice yield is expected to increase by 5 to 10 per cent this year compared to the previous year, supported by favourable rainfall and better crop conditions, according to Rajeev Setia, President, Basmati IREF, and Joint Managing Director, Chaman Lal Setia Exports Ltd.

Speaking to ANI on the sidelines of the Bharat International Rice Conference 2026 in New Delhi, Setia said the monsoon and subsequent rainfall had supported the growth of the basmati crop, resulting in expectations of higher yields.

"The monsoon was reasonable... and thereafter there were good rains. Just look around, greenery we have all around. So in that way the crop grew and the yield in this particular year for basmati rice is higher," he said.

Asked about the expected increase, Setia said, "It will definitely be 5-10%... higher as compared to the preceding year." The expected improvement in yields is significant for India's basmati rice industry, as higher agricultural productivity could support export availability amid expectations of growing international demand.

Setia also expressed optimism about the long-term demand for Indian basmati rice, pointing to the increasing popularity of Indian food across international markets. "The requirement of Basmati is likely to grow in the time to come," he told ANI. He said Indian basmati rice has established a presence across international markets, while his own company exports to 96 countries.

Setia noted that the growing popularity of Indian cuisine among consumers in Europe and the United States is helping expand the market for basmati rice beyond traditional consumers. He also highlighted India's position in the global basmati rice trade, noting that the crop has geographical indication (GI) recognition and is cultivated in specific geographical regions.

India is one of the world's leading producers and exporters of basmati rice, with the crop playing an important role in the country's agricultural exports. Higher yields could improve supply availability, although actual export performance will also depend on international demand and market conditions.

The Bharat International Rice Conference 2026 is being held from October 23 to 25 in New Delhi, bringing together Indian exporters, international buyers and other stakeholders in the global rice trade.

events.headline: Global slump: Why corporate capex in India is unlikely to rise just yet

items.title: Global slump: Why corporate capex in India is unlikely to rise just yet
items.summary: Capital expenditure by corporate firms has been weak in much of the world. But India's total investment-to-GDP ratio has been better than pre-covid and is second only to China. That said, global policy flux and unfavourable government capex weigh against strong pick-up.

events.article_text:
In the previous two parts of this series, I established that:

1) India’s corporate profits have been stable at 9-10% of gross domestic product (GDP), though its composition has changed in favour of the listed sector

2) lower household savings, higher fiscal deficit and narrower current account deficit (CAD) have supported profits, despite lower corporate capex and

3) India’s unlisted sector is huge, accounting for about two-thirds of the aggregate corporate sector in terms of capex, debt and gross value added (GVA), though its financial position has worsened in the post-pandemic period, hurting aggregate corporate capex.

In this final part, my key conclusions are two-fold: first, weak corporate capex is not a unique phenomenon in India. Second, considering various cyclical and structural factors, we don’t expect corporate capex to pick-up anytime soon.

Note that India’s corporate capex has been stable at 14-15% of GDP in the past decade, lower than the 17-18% in the post-2008 period and its peak of 21% in 2007-08. That makes it the lowest level in almost two decades, but it is not low compared to most other major economies.

While China has had the highest corporate capex at 26% of GDP in recent years, followed by Indonesia, South Korea and Japan (20%-plus), it is between 12-14% for others such as the UK, Germany, the Philippines, US and Spain.

Importantly, India’s total investment-to-GDP ratio has averaged 33% in recent years. Not only is this better than about 30% in the pre-pandemic period, but also only second to China’s 40% among the world’s major economies.

These two facts suggest that the share of the corporate sector has fallen from above 50% a decade ago to about 45% in India’s total investments, while the share of the household sector (primarily consisting of the residential property market) has risen to 42-43%, with a 12-13% share of the government sector.

Since corporate capex is the most efficient, its lower share does hit the overall efficiency of India’s total investments. However, the quantity of total investments remains healthy in India owing to strong household capex.

Notably, the surge in China’s total investment-to-GDP ratio from 35% at the turn of the century to its peak of 46% in the early 2010s was largely led by the household sector, whose capex more than doubled to a peak of 15% of GDP.

The corporate capex boom remains one of the most widely held expectations for India, which is yet to materialize. However, the absence of a pick-up is not unique to India. Using data on other major economies (such as China, euro-zone, Japan, South Korea, UK and US), together accounting for 70% of global GDP, we create annual data on global profits and corporate capex.

The results are staggering. Global corporate capex has increased to 17% of GDP in the 2020s decade (2020-24) from 16.1% in the 2010s decade and 14.4% in the 2000s, while global profits have increased every decade from 6.1% of GDP in the 1990s to 8% in the 2000s and about 9% in the post-pandemic period.

However, the conclusion changes dramatically if we exclude China from the global aggregates. Although the rise in global profits is starker now—from 6% of GDP in the 1990s to 9.6% in the 2020s decade, global corporate capex has been actually stagnant at about 14% of GDP during the past two decades or so.

China, thus, is an exception, where profit is falling with rising corporate capex. Global corporate capex excluding China has been largely stagnant in the past two decades, despite much higher profits.

Similarly, India’s prolonged corporate debt deleveraging episode in the recent decade was neither unique nor exceptional. Corporate debt fell from its peak of 70% of GDP in 2011-12 in India to a low of 48% in 2023-24, after which it has picked up towards 50%.

According to data on 43 countries from the Bank for International Settlements, there were 68 episodes of corporate deleveraging during the four decades up to 2007, of which only 11 were deep and prolonged cycles, lasting seven years or more. Since 2007, however, there have been at least 19 such deleveraging episodes, majority of which are still incomplete.

Further, while corporate credit growth has picked-up in recent quarters, other drivers such as global policy uncertainty, government capex and profit growth remain unfavourable. Therefore, we don’t expect any strong pick-up in India’s corporate capex over the next few years.

Can AI-led capex change that? Notwithstanding the news of hundreds of billions of dollars invested by US tech giants, its total investment-to-GDP ratio was unchanged at 21.5% in recent years. The US’s total corporate capex has also been stable at 13.7% of GDP. Moreover, US corporate debt was at a decade low of 48.7% of GDP in the second quarter of calendar year 2026.

Not only the US, but the total investment-to-GDP ratio has been lower-to-stable in China, Singapore, South Korea and the UK. Taiwan and Japan are exceptions, with increases. If so, the case for AI-driven global capex recovery needs more scrutiny.

But what if corporate capex, and thus, the total investment-to-GDP ratio picks up? In that case, policymakers will have to shift their focus towards ensuring sustainable funding of higher investment.

The Indian economy has seen three episodes of a rise in investment-to-GDP ratio since the 1980s. During all these, the increase in savings lagged that in investment, leading to a wider CAD. Worryingly, the deterioration in CAD has accelerated over the decades. Therefore, if the investment-to-GDP ratio starts rising further, low household savings will become a key concern, as CAD will widen and constrain investment growth.

What else can be done to push growth higher? The quality of investment (or efficiency) must improve. Most successful economies have achieved high real GDP growth for decades with a lower investment-to-GDP ratio but better efficiency. Between 2003-04 and 2025-26, India’s incremental capital-output ratio

analysis.tldr: Expect corporate investments in India to stay slow for a while, meaning job creation and manufacturing expansion will lean heavily on the government and households rather than big private companies.
the_story: India's corporate capex (spending on long-term assets like factories and equipment) has stayed stable at 14-15% of GDP in the past decade, down from a peak of 21% in 2007-08.
Global corporate capex excluding China has been stagnant at about 14% of GDP for the past two decades, showing that India's slow corporate spending is part of a wider global trend.
India's total investment-to-GDP ratio averages a healthy 33%, but the corporate sector's share has dropped to 45% while households (mainly housing) have risen to 42-43%.
India's corporate debt (borrowing by companies) fell from a peak of 70% of GDP in 2011-12 to 48% in 2023-24, before ticking up towards 50%.
Factors like global policy uncertainty, government spending limits, and profit growth mean analysts do not expect a strong pick-up in India's corporate capex over the next few years.
analysis.what_happened: An analysis of global and Indian economic data shows that companies everywhere are holding back on heavy spending, and India is no exception. While Indian companies have spent the last decade paying down old debts rather than building new plants, global corporate spending outside of China has also stayed flat for twenty years despite high profits.
analysis.analogy: It is like a group of shop owners who finally paid off their old store loans, but instead of expanding and opening new branches right away, they are keeping cash in reserve because the global market feels too uncertain.
why_it_matters_india: Private companies keep capex low due to global uncertainty and recent debt cleanup -> factories and industrial capacity expand more slowly.
Household real estate and government spending prop up overall investment -> total economic growth remains decent despite weak corporate spending.
If corporate spending eventually surges, low domestic savings could cause the current account deficit (when a country imports more than it exports in value) to widen.
A wider deficit can strain the economy, meaning future growth relies more on boosting business efficiency than just spending more money.

impacts.rationale: Without a rapid surge in corporate expansion and factory building, big listed companies may see slower profit acceleration, which can weigh on stock market enthusiasm.
Slower private sector investment means less sudden overheating in industrial demand, which generally keeps runaway price rises in check — good for household budgets.
If a future investment boom outpaces local savings, a widening trade and current account gap can put downward pressure on the currency, making imports pricier.

watch_next: Whether household savings rates begin to recover from recent lows
Updates on government capital spending plans in upcoming budgets
Trends in corporate credit growth from banks
analysis.caveats: If new artificial intelligence technologies or sudden global demand triggers an unexpected, massive wave of factory building worldwide, local companies might change their plans faster than expected.

events.headline: Federal Reserve Board releases results of the 2025 Survey of Consumer Finances, which provides the public and policymakers with detailed insights into the economic condition of American families

items.title: Federal Reserve Board releases results of the 2025 Survey of Consumer Finances, which provides the public and policymakers with detailed insights into the economic condition of American families
items.summary: Federal Reserve Board releases results of the 2025 Survey of Consumer Finances, which provides the public and policymakers with detailed insights into the economic condition of American families

events.article_text:
An official website of the United States Government

Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock () or https:// means you've safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

The Federal Reserve Board on Friday released the results of the 2025 Survey of Consumer Finances, which provides the public and policymakers with detailed insights into the economic condition of American families.

The data provide a representative picture of what Americans own, how and how much they borrow, and how they bank. The current version of the survey has been undertaken every three years since 1989 and provides the public with an extensive time series of thorough information on the economic conditions of American families. Alongside the survey data, the Board issued its summary report entitled Changes in U.S. Family Finances from 2022 to 2025 (PDF), which examines changes in income, net worth, assets, debt, and financial vulnerability.

In addition to the summary report, an interactive chartbook displaying changes in these financial characteristics over time is available here. Additional data from the survey, including extensive data examining other economic conditions of American families, is made available to researchers and the public here.

The survey is conducted for the Board by NORC, a social science research organization at the University of Chicago. Participants in the study are chosen at random from 119 geographic areas, including metropolitan areas and rural counties across the United States, using scientific sampling procedures that aim to produce a sample representative of American families.

For media inquiries, please email [email protected] or call (202) 452-2955.

Changes in U.S. Family Finances from 2022 to 2025 Evidence from the Survey of Consumer Finances (PDF)

analysis.tldr: This U.S. consumer financial survey is a data-gathering report that has no direct or immediate impact on Indian savings, loans, or the rupee.
the_story: The Federal Reserve Board released the 2025 Survey of Consumer Finances on Friday to show the economic condition of American families.
The survey covers what Americans own, how much they borrow, and how they bank, based on a recurring study done every three years since 1989.
The Board also issued a summary report called Changes in U.S. Family Finances from 2022 to 2025 detailing income, net worth, assets, and debt.
The survey was conducted by NORC, a research organization at the University of Chicago, using randomly chosen participants from across the United States.
analysis.what_happened: The U.S. central bank published a routine, periodic research report detailing the financial health, assets, and debts of American households. This report is produced every three years to help policymakers understand consumer finances, caused by ongoing data collection efforts rather than a sudden economic emergency.
analysis.analogy: It is like a nationwide health check-up for a large household, recording their weight and blood pressure every three years to see how they have changed, rather than prescribing urgent medicine.
why_it_matters_india: The U.S. Federal Reserve (America's central bank) releases a survey on American household finances.
The report is purely informational data for researchers and policymakers to study U.S. trends.
Because this contains no new policy changes or interest rate announcements, it does not change financial conditions.
Therefore, there is no direct transmission channel to Indian inflation, currency markets, or specific stock prices.

impacts.rationale: Since this is a domestic U.S. statistical report without monetary policy changes, it will likely leave currency markets completely unmoved.
Global stock markets react to interest rates and earnings, not statistical background surveys on consumer debt, meaning zero impact on Indian share prices.

watch_next: U.S. Federal Reserve interest rate announcements
analysis.caveats: Only the headline and text of a routine statistical release were available, confirming it contains purely historical survey data with no policy action.

events.headline: Japan Needs Higher Interest Rates

items.title: Japan Needs Higher Interest Rates
items.summary: Japanese exporters enjoy high demand and strong profit margins, but importers are under severe pressure. The weak yen also hurts Japanese consumers.

events.article_text:
On a recent visit to Sapporo, the city on Japan’s northern island where my parents came from, my wife and I found gentle people, mild autumn days, and excellent food. As tourists who live and work in the United States, we also enjoyed very low prices: lunch at a high-quality restaurant cost only about $20 per person. While that was convenient for us, like so many other tourists who have headed to Japan to take advantage of favorable exchange rates, the cheap yen (yen yasu) has been hard on Japan’s economy.

To understand the pressure Japan is under, it is worth looking at the purchasing-power-parity equilibrium exchange rate – the rate at which a representative basket of goods and services would cost the same across two countries. This month, the OECD reports a PPP equilibrium exchange rate between Japan and the United States of around 93 yen per dollar. That is a far cry from the actual yen-dollar exchange rate, which has been hovering in the 150–160 range.

This means that goods produced in Japan cost much less than goods produced in the United States. As a result, Japanese exporters enjoy high demand and strong profit margins, but importers are under severe pressure. The weak yen also hurts Japanese consumers, as it creates strong incentives to raise prices: With imported goods more expensive, domestic producers know that their output will find buyers, and importers might pass their mounting costs on to buyers.

Japan used to have the opposite problem. In the early 1980s, it was a dominant economy experiencing strong growth. But the 1985 Plaza Accord, under which major economies agreed to take coordinated action to strengthen their currencies vis-à-vis the U.S. dollar, changed everything. After the accord was implemented, the PPP exchange rate was higher than the actual exchange rate, reaching almost double in 1995.

The strong yen (yen daka) persisted for decades, contributing to chronic deflation and stagnant growth. During this period, a visit to Tokyo strained tourists’ pocketbooks, Japanese goods found few customers abroad, and Japan’s once-formidable industries struggled. The situation deteriorated further around the 2008 global economic crisis, when the United States embraced monetary easing.

In the decades after the Plaza Accord, Bank of Japan (BOJ) governors (with the possible exception of Fukui Toshihiko) consistently failed to loosen monetary policy in line with changing economic conditions. Deflationary pressures intensified.

After returning to power in 2012, Prime Minister Abe Shinzo sought to turn things around with an economic-reform package, which came to be known as Abenomics. (I served as an adviser to Abe.) This package included a recommendation for monetary expansion, which then-BOJ Governor Kuroda Haruhiko embraced.

Now, conditions have changed. After the COVID-19 pandemic, the United States experienced a surge in inflation, which forced the U.S. Federal Reserve to abandon monetary expansion and raise interest rates. As the dollar strengthened, and the Japan-U.S. interest-rate differential widened, the yen depreciated in value, and deflationary forces gave way to inflationary pressures.

When circumstances change, so, too, must policy. For the BOJ today, this means pursuing monetary tightening in order to reduce the domestic money supply, and raising the interest rate.

To some extent, Japanese policymakers seem to recognize this. After keeping the short-term interest rate around 1 percent for some time, the BOJ raised its policy rate to 1.25 percent last month. This is high for Japan – the highest in 31 years, to be precise. But with the U.S. short-term money market pushing the interest rate close to 4 percent, and more U.S. rate hikes likely, it is not nearly enough. Speculators continue to exploit the interest-rate differential via the so-called carry trade (borrowing cheaply in yen to invest in higher-yielding assets abroad).

Under the gold standard or a fixed exchange rate, if a major country pursued monetary expansion, another, weaker country might need to reduce its money supply and raise its interest rate. Under a flexible exchange-rate regime, however, an expansion in one country should be met with a (moderate) expansion in another, just as tightening should be met with tightening.

We know that U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Japanese Finance Minister Katayama Satsuki are communicating about fiscal and monetary matters. Ultimately, however, monetary policy must be pursued autonomously, with BOJ Governor Ueda Kazuo doing what is best for Japan’s economy. Under the current circumstances, that means reducing the money supply and raising interest rates more aggressively.

analysis.tldr: Japan is raising its very low interest rates to fix its weak currency, which could push global investors to pull borrowed money out of emerging markets like India.
the_story: The yen (Japanese currency) is trading around 150 to 160 per U.S. dollar, far weaker than the OECD's fair-value estimate of about 93 yen per dollar.
This weak yen makes imported goods expensive for Japanese consumers and puts pressure on the domestic economy, even though Japanese exporters benefit.
The Bank of Japan (BOJ, Japan's central bank) recently raised its policy interest rate to 1.25 percent, its highest level in 31 years.
However, with U.S. interest rates close to 4 percent, speculators are still doing the carry trade (borrowing cheaply in yen to invest in higher-yielding assets abroad).
The author argues that BOJ Governor Ueda Kazuo needs to reduce the money supply and raise interest rates even more aggressively.
analysis.what_happened: Japan's central bank kept interest rates extremely low for a long time. But after the U.S. raised its interest rates to fight inflation, money flowed toward the U.S., causing the Japanese yen to drop heavily in value and creating local price pressures. To fix this, Japan has started raising its interest rates.
analysis.analogy: It is like a local shopkeeper who kept their prices frozen for years while everyone else raised theirs, and now they are forced to catch up quickly so they do not run out of money.
why_it_matters_india: Japan raises its interest rates -> borrowing in cheap yen becomes less attractive for global investors.
Investors unwind the carry trade -> they sell off risky foreign assets, including Indian stocks and bonds, to repay their cheap yen loans.
Foreign money flows out of India -> FIIs (big foreign investors) pull capital back to Japan or developed markets.
Capital outflows hit Indian markets -> pressure builds on Indian stock indices and the rupee.

impacts.rationale: If global investors have to pay back their cheap Japanese loans, they pull money out of emerging markets like India, which can drag down stock prices — bad for everyday investors.
When foreign money leaves India, the demand for rupees drops, weakening the currency — bad because it makes imported items like crude oil and electronics more expensive for Indians.

watch_next: Further interest rate hikes by the Bank of Japan
How fast global speculators close out their yen-funded investments
analysis.caveats: If the Bank of Japan raises interest rates much slower than expected, global investors might keep borrowing cheap yen for longer, delaying any sudden shock to Indian markets.

events.article_text:
Utssav CZ Gold Jewels Ltd has approved a 1:1 bonus share issue that would double its paid-up equity share capital to ₹49.996 crore, subject to shareholders' approval and other regulatory clearances.

The company's board approved the proposal on October 23 to issue one fully paid-up equity share of ₹10 each for every existing share held by eligible shareholders, the jewellery manufacturer said in a statement.

The proposed issue will comprise 2.5 crore bonus shares, increasing the total number of equity shares to 5 crore from 2.5 crore. The company's paid-up equity share capital will rise from ₹24.998 crore to ₹49.996 crore following the issue.

The bonus shares will be issued from the company's securities premium, free reserves and retained earnings available as of March 31, 2026. The shares are expected to be credited within 60 days of the board's approval, subject to the requisite shareholder and regulatory clearances.

The company has yet to announce the record date, which will determine shareholders eligible to receive the bonus shares.

The board also approved a proposal to increase authorised share capital to ₹60 crore from ₹24.998 crore, divided into 6 crore equity shares of ₹10 each. The move, which also requires shareholder approval, would provide headroom for the proposed expansion of the company's paid-up capital.

A bonus issue increases the number of shares held by existing shareholders without requiring them to make an additional payment. While the number of shares held by each eligible investor would double under the proposed 1:1 issue, the investor's proportional ownership would remain unchanged, all else being equal. The issue does not, by itself, increase the company's underlying business value or shareholders' aggregate investment value.

Utssav CZ Gold Jewels manufactures, wholesales and exports lightweight cubic zirconia and gold-casting jewellery.

(Only the headline and picture of this report may have been reworked by the Business Standard staff; the rest of the content is auto-generated from a syndicated feed.)

analysis.tldr: A jewellery company giving out free bonus shares changes the count of shares you own, but it doesn't automatically make your overall investment worth more money.
the_story: On October 23, the board of Utssav CZ Gold Jewels Ltd approved a 1:1 bonus share issue.
Eligible shareholders will get one new free share worth ₹10 for every existing share they hold, doubling the total shares from 2.5 crore to 5 crore.
The company's paid-up equity share capital (total money raised by issuing shares) will rise from ₹24.998 crore to ₹49.996 crore.
The bonus shares will be paid for using the company's existing securities premium, free reserves, and retained earnings (profits kept back by the business) as of March 31, 2026.
The board also approved increasing the authorized share capital (the maximum capital a company is allowed to raise) to ₹60 crore.
analysis.what_happened: Utssav CZ Gold Jewels decided to reward its current shareholders by doubling the number of shares they hold without asking them to pay any extra money. They are funding this by using savings and profits the company has stacked up over time. This plan still needs formal approval from the shareholders and regulators.
analysis.analogy: It is like cutting a single pizza into 8 slices instead of 4. You have more pieces in your box now, but the actual amount of pizza you can eat remains exactly the same.
why_it_matters_india: A company announces a 1:1 bonus share issue using its accumulated profits.
Existing shareholders see the number of shares they own double in their demat accounts (digital lockers for shares).
Because the total value of the company hasn't changed, the price of each individual share typically adjusts downward to balance out the extra supply.
Retail investors (individual everyday people investing small amounts) sometimes mistake this share multiplication for extra wealth, leading to short-term trading excitement.

impacts.target: Stock price of Utssav CZ Gold Jewels
impacts.rationale: When a company issues bonus shares, the stock price generally splits or adjusts downward because the company's total value is now spread across twice as many shares.
This is a single small company's internal corporate action and has virtually no impact on the broader Indian stock market.

watch_next: The announcement of the record date (the cut-off date to decide which investors qualify for the bonus shares)
Whether shareholders approve the plan during their upcoming vote
analysis.caveats: The bonus issue is still subject to getting formal approval from shareholders and regulatory authorities.

events.headline: Designing an AI serving harness built to last

items.title: Designing an AI serving harness built to last
items.summary: The next competitive advantage in enterprise AI has less to do with which model you choose than with what you build around it. That’s an important shift. For the past several years, much of the AI conversation has centered on model capability: bigger models, better reasoning, larger context windows, higher benchmark scores. Those advances have…

events.article_text:
The next competitive advantage in enterprise AI has less to do with which model you choose than with what you build around it.

That’s an important shift. For the past several years, much of the AI conversation has centered on model capability: bigger models, better reasoning, larger context windows, higher benchmark scores. Those advances have been extraordinary. But as AI moves from experimentation to production, the question facing enterprise leaders has changed—it’s no longer, “what can the model do?”—it’s now, “Can we deliver that intelligence reliably, economically, and at scale?”

Increasingly, the answer depends on the serving harness—the engineering system surrounding the model, including the architecture, memory management, scheduling, and optimization decisions that determine how efficiently model intelligence becomes a production capability.

For technical executives, that changes where AI investment should go—and what they should demand from the architecture supporting it.

There is no universally “best” model or AI architecture. There is only the right solution for the business problem.

A customer-facing assistant optimized for fast responses has fundamentally different requirements from a document-processing pipeline that can run overnight. An internal knowledge application and a high-volume customer service platform may use the same foundation model but require very different serving architectures.

The workload defines the constraints. The constraints should determine the architecture.

That sounds simple, but it runs counter to the way many organizations have approached early AI deployments. During a proof of concept, model accuracy naturally dominates the discussion. Production introduces constraints that are much easier to ignore when only a handful of users are involved: latency, concurrency, memory pressure, GPU utilization, infrastructure cost, and unpredictable traffic.

A model that produces marginally better answers is not necessarily the better production choice if it doubles inference costs or cannot meet the application's latency requirements. Not every workload needs a Ferrari. Sometimes the smarter engineering decision is the model that delivers exactly the performance the business needs without paying for capability it doesn't.

The objective should be to deploy the right intelligence at the right cost for the workload. That makes serving architecture more than an engineering concern. It becomes an investment decision: where to spend on compute, where to optimize, and where additional model capability simply isn't worth the cost.

Once AI reaches production, seemingly isolated engineering decisions begin affecting one another. Serving architecture influences memory utilization. Memory management affects concurrency. Concurrency shapes batching and scheduling, and scheduling affects GPU utilization and latency.

Only then can techniques such as quantization, speculative decoding, or optimized attention mechanisms deliver their full value. This interdependence matters because organizations can spend considerably more on infrastructure without solving the constraint limiting performance.

GPU memory is a good example. During inference, the model's weights remain fixed, but the key-value (KV) cache grows with active requests and context length. As concurrency increases, a system can run short of usable GPU memory even when compute capacity is still available. Adding more compute without understanding that bottleneck may simply make an inefficient system more expensive.

The lesson for technology leaders is broader than memory management: Measure before you optimize. Identify the dominant constraint. Address it. Measure the result. Then determine if another bottleneck emerged. Repeat.

Don't think of optimization techniques as Pokémon cards: The goal isn't to collect them all. The goal is to apply the technique that removes the highest-impact constraint while preserving the application's business requirements.

For technology leaders, that demands a different governance question. Instead of asking which AI capabilities the organization can deploy, ask which constraints stand between a proven capability and sustainable business value.

Perhaps the most important reason to invest in the serving harness is that today's leading model will probably not be tomorrow’s. Models will improve. Hardware will evolve. New optimization techniques will emerge. The architecture surrounding them should make those changes easier to absorb, not force the enterprise to rebuild its AI platform every time technology advances.

That makes adaptability an increasingly important outcome of AI strategy.

Organizations that build serving systems around workload requirements, clear service-level objectives, and measurable production economics gain the ability to evaluate new models and infrastructure against what the business actually needs. A model change can become an evaluation and configuration decision rather than an architectural reset.

EXL researchers have explored these production challenges in greater depth in the EXL Engineering the Harness series. It examines how serving architecture, memory management, scheduling, and inference optimization work together to make enterprise AI more efficient, scalable, and economically sustainable.

Increasingly, enterprises have access to many of the same models. Sustainable differentiation comes from how effectively an organization turns that intelligence into business outcomes.

The model provides the intelligence. The harness determines whether the enterprise can deliver outcomes reliably, economically, and at scale.

This content was produced by EXL. It was not written by MIT Technology Review’s editorial staff.

Ten years after AlphaGo’s match against Go champion Lee Sedol, today’s AI still isn’t tapping into the machinery that made that win possible.

An exclusive interview with Nick Cammarata, the researcher whose 26,000-word viral blo

analysis.tldr: Businesses using AI must focus on building efficient engineering systems rather than just buying the smartest AI models, which will change how tech companies spend their money and manage hardware costs.
the_story: Enterprise AI strategy is shifting focus from raw model capability (like bigger models and better reasoning) to the 'serving harness'—the engineering systems surrounding the model.
The serving harness includes architecture, memory management, scheduling, and optimization decisions that dictate how efficiently AI runs in production.

Different business workloads (such as a fast customer-facing assistant versus an overnight document processor) require fundamentally different serving architectures tailored to specific constraints like latency and cost.
Poor architectural choices can waste money; for example, adding more computing hardware without fixing GPU memory bottlenecks for active requests simply makes an inefficient system more expensive.
Investing in a flexible serving harness helps companies easily swap out models or upgrade hardware in the future without having to completely rebuild their AI platforms.
analysis.what_happened: As artificial intelligence moves from early experimentation into real-world business production, companies are realizing that having the smartest AI model isn't enough. The article explains that success now depends on the 'serving harness'—the underlying computer systems and memory management that deliver AI intelligence economically and at scale. This sponsored content piece by EXL highlights that businesses must design their engineering setups based on specific workloads rather than just chasing the most advanced models.
analysis.analogy: It is like buying a high-end sports car: having a powerful engine (the AI model) does not matter if your garage door is too small and your driveway is full of potholes (the serving harness), because you will never get a smooth or cost-effective ride.
why_it_matters_india: Indian IT services and enterprise tech companies build and manage AI applications for global clients.
A shift toward cost-efficient AI serving harnesses means Indian tech firms must optimize cloud computing infrastructure and memory management for clients.
Better engineering practices lower the high costs of running AI inference (running trained models in real-time).
Lower infrastructure costs make enterprise AI adoption more affordable, potentially driving higher tech spending volumes for Indian outsourcing and software providers.

impacts.target: IT stocks like TCS, Infosys, and Wipro
impacts.rationale: Focusing on enterprise AI engineering and serving harnesses creates new high-value consulting and tech deployment contracts for Indian IT giants — generally good for tech investors.
More efficient AI infrastructure lowers business operating costs economy-wide, reducing upward pressure on consumer prices — good for everyone.

watch_next: How enterprise tech budgets shift toward infrastructure optimization versus buying raw AI model access
Further research publications from firms like EXL on engineering AI serving architectures
analysis.caveats: This text was produced as sponsored content by EXL and primarily reflects a corporate enterprise tech perspective rather than a broad macroeconomic shift.

history.title: When the safest thing in finance turned out not to be
history.what: American house prices fell, mortgage securities that were rated as safe as government bonds proved worthless, and Lehman Brothers was allowed to fail. Global credit markets stopped functioning within days.
history.why: Mortgages were bundled into securities, sliced into tranches, and rated AAA on the assumption that house prices would never fall across the whole country at once. That assumption had held for decades, so it was treated as a law. Banks held these with very little of their own capital behind them, and insured each other through derivatives — which concentrated the risk rather than spreading it.
history.impact: Global shares fell more than 50%. World trade collapsed faster than in 1929. Unemployment doubled in the US and Europe. India's Sensex fell about 60% and the rupee slid sharply, despite Indian banks holding almost none of the toxic assets — a pure demonstration that a foreign-funded market imports foreign panic.
history.policy: Bank bailouts, then zero interest rates and quantitative easing — central banks creating money to buy bonds — on a scale never attempted before. Regulation followed: Basel III forced banks to hold far more capital, and Dodd-Frank restricted what they could trade with their own money.
history.consequence: Banks became safer and far less profitable, and much risky lending simply migrated to less-regulated non-bank lenders — where it still sits. A decade of near-zero rates inflated the price of every asset and widened wealth inequality sharply, which reshaped the politics of the following decade.
history.pattern: The dangerous asset is never the one everybody calls risky. It is the one everybody calls safe, because that is where leverage accumulates unexamined. Ask what today's "obviously safe" holding is, and what would have to be true for it not to be.
history.india_echo: India's own version arrived in 2018 when IL&FS, rated AAA, defaulted and froze the entire non-bank lending sector. Same shape: a AAA rating, heavy short-term borrowing funding long-term assets, and a regulator watching the wrong institution.
history.watch_for: Ratings doing the thinking for investors. When a security is bought because of its rating rather than its cash flows, the rating is the risk.
